text: The Henry Draper Catalogue (HD) is an astronomical star catalogue published between 1918 and 1924, providing spectroscopic classifications for 225,300 stars; it was later expanded by the Henry Draper Extension (HDE), published between 1925 and 1936, which added classifications for 46,850 more stars, and by the Henry Draper Extension Charts (HDEC), published from 1937 to 1949 in the form of charts, which provided classifications for 86,933 additional stars. In total, 359,083 stars were classified as of August 2017. The HD catalogue is named after Henry Draper, an amateur astronomer, and covers the entire sky almost completely down to an apparent photographic magnitude of about 9; the extensions added fainter stars in certain areas of the sky. The construction of the Henry Draper Catalogue was part of a pioneering effort to classify stellar spectra, and its catalogue numbers are commonly used to identify stars. The origin of the catalogue dates back to Henry Draper's first photograph of a star's spectrum, Vega, in 1872, followed by over a hundred more stellar spectrum photographs before his death in 1882. In 1885, Edward Pickering began supervising photographic spectroscopy at the Harvard College Observatory using the objective prism method; in 1886, Draper's widow, Mary Anna Palmer Draper, funded the work under the name Henry Draper Memorial. Pickering and his team began an objective-prism survey of the sky and classified the resulting spectra. A first result was the Draper Catalogue of Stellar Spectra, published in 1890, which included spectroscopic classifications for 10,351 stars, mostly north of declination −25°, with most classifications done by Williamina Fleming. The classification scheme subdivided the Secchi classes (I to IV) into letters A to N, with O for stars with bright lines, P for planetary nebulae, and Q for spectra not fitting into classes A through P; no star of type N appeared, and the only star of type O was HR 2583. Antonia Maury and Pickering published a more detailed study of bright northern hemisphere stars in 1897, using classifications from I to XXII, with groups I to XX corresponding to subdivisions of Draper types B, A, F, G, K, and M, and XXI and XXII corresponding to types N and O; she was the first to place B stars before A stars. In 1890, the Harvard College Observatory built the Boyden Observatory in Arequipa, Peru to study the southern sky, and in 1901, Annie Jump Cannon and Pickering published a study of bright southern hemisphere stars. Cannon used the Draper Catalogue's lettered types but dropped all letters except O, B, A, F, G, K, and M in that order, plus P for planetary nebulae and Q for peculiar spectra, and introduced types such as B5A for stars halfway between B and A, F2G for stars one-fifth of the way from F to G, and so on. Between 1910 and 1915, increased interest in stellar classification led to the start of work on the Henry Draper Catalogue in 1911, with Cannon and her coworkers classifying spectra at a rate of approximately 5,000 per month from 1912 to 1915. The catalogue was published in nine volumes of the Annals of Harvard College Observatory between 1918 and 1924, containing rough positions, magnitudes, spectral classifications, and cross-references to the Durchmusterung catalogs for 225,300 stars. The classification scheme was similar to Cannon's 1901 work, but types such as B, A, B5A, F2G were changed to B0, A0, B5, F2, and so on, with classes O through M, P for nebulae, and R and N for carbon stars. Pickering died on February 3, 1919, leaving six volumes to be overseen by Cannon. She classified 46,850 fainter stars in selected regions of the sky in the Henry Draper Extension, published in six parts between 1925 and 1936. She continued classifying stars until her death in 1941; most of these classifications were published in 1949 in the Henry Draper Extension Charts (the first portion of which was published in 1937), with Margaret Walton Mayall supervising the work after Cannon's death. The catalogue and its extensions were the first large-scale attempt to catalogue stellar spectral types and led to the Harvard classification scheme, still used today. Stars in the main catalogue are of medium magnitude, down to about 9th magnitude (about 1/15 as bright as the faintest stars visible to the naked eye), while the extensions include stars as faint as the 11th magnitude in selected sky regions. Stars in the original catalogue are numbered from 1 to 225,300 (prefix HD), in order of increasing right ascension for the epoch 1900.0; the first extension stars are numbered from 225,301 to 272,150 (prefix HDE); extension chart stars are numbered from 272,151 to 359,083 (prefix HDEC). However, the numbering is continuous, so the prefix HD may be used without ambiguity. Many stars are commonly identified by their HD numbers. The Henry Draper Catalogue and Extension were available from the NASA Astronomical Data Center as part of their third CD-ROM of astronomical catalogues and are currently available from the VizieR service of the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg as catalogue number III/135A. Due to their format, converting the Henry Draper Extension Charts into a machine-readable format was difficult, but it was completed by 1995 by Nesterov, Röser and their coworkers, and the charts are now available at VizieR as catalogue number III/182. The Henry Draper Catalogue and its extensions are available online free of charge at the VizieR service of the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg.
